chain.g: a divided game, i.e. an even game, an even chance

ety.text: From Middle English jupartie, jeupartie (“even chance”), from Anglo-Norman giu parti and Middle French jeu parti (“a divided game, i.e. an even game, an even chance”), from Medieval Latin iocus partītus (“an even chance, an alternative”), from Latin iocus (“jest, play, game”) + partītus, perfect passive participle of partiō (“divide”); see joke and party.

senses.d: Danger of failure, harm, or loss.
ex: The poor condition of the vehicle put its occupants in constant jeopardy.

grp.label: danger of failure, harm, or loss

ety.text: Inherited from Old French dangier, alteration of Old French dongier (due to association with Latin damnum (“damage”)), from Vulgar Latin *domniārium (“authority, power”), from Latin dominus (“lord, master”).
Inherited from Old French peril, from Vulgar Latin *periclu(m), syncopated form of Latin perīculum.
Inherited from Middle French risque (first attested in 1578), borrowed from Old Italian risco (modern Italian rischio).
Borrowed from Latin perīculum. Doublet of the archaic inherited periglio.

Latin resecōdeverb. Vulgar Latin *resecum Old Italian risco Italian rischio From Old Italian risco, from Vulgar Latin *resecum or deverbal from resecare, via risicare and later riscare, rischiare, both from Latin resecō (“to cut off”). Compare Sicilian rìsicu.

Latin perīculumslbor. Old Spanish periglo Old Spanish peligro Spanish peligro Inherited from Old Spanish peligro, metathesized from earlier periglo, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin perīculum. The expected inherited result would have been *perijo; compare the similar phonetic evolution of milagro.

es:riesgo.gl: risk; the possibility of harm or an unfavorable outcome from random chance

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish riesco, possibly from Vulgar Latin *resecum, deverbal of Latin resecō. Doublet of risco.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perigoo, probably a semi-learned word from Latin perīculum (“danger”). Compare Galician perigo and Spanish peligro.
